summary: Argues that IPv6 does not need NAT to get the benefits people often attribute to it, such as some management and security properties. It describes how to get local network protection in IPv6 using other mechanisms, such as firewalls and address planning. It is informational.

eli5.summary: People say hiding houses behind a shared front door keeps them safe. This note shows you can be safe with proper locks and fences, without the shared door trick.

questions: how to protect a local network with ipv6
how do ipv6 privacy addresses work
how to hide network topology in ipv6
subtitle: How to protect IPv6 networks without network address translation

tldr.problem: Networks need protection and management features that are often associated with NAT in IPv4, but NAT is not necessary in IPv6 because of its large address space.
tldr.mechanism: IPv6 provides several built-in tools: firewalls with reflexive access control, privacy addresses that hide device identity, unique local addresses for local networks, and topology masking techniques.
tldr.outcome: Networks can achieve the same security and management benefits as IPv4 NAT without address translation, preserving end-to-end transparency and application functionality.

facts.label: Time to scan one /64
facts.value: Over 5,000 years at 40 Gbps full rate

today: RFC 4864 is informational and remains current guidance on IPv6 network design. IPv6 deployment is increasing, and the techniques described (ULAs, privacy addresses, firewall-based security) are in active use in production networks. NAT is not required for IPv6, and modern IPv6 networks typically use the approaches outlined here instead.

sections.title: Why IPv6 Does Not Need NAT
sections.content:
IPv4 networks widely use NAT because the address space is limited and administrators want security and management features. However, IPv6 was designed to make NAT unnecessary. This document shows how Local Network Protection (LNP) techniques in IPv6 provide the same or better management and security without address translation.

The key difference is that IPv6 has a vastly larger address space, so address scarcity is not a problem. Instead, networks use a combination of techniques: firewalls for simple security, privacy addresses to hide device identity, unique local addresses for network autonomy, and topology masking for privacy.

NAT does provide some artifacts that are valuable—stateful filtering, topology hiding, and independence from ISP addressing—but IPv6 achieves these benefits through explicit, well-understood mechanisms rather than header modification.
sections.eli5: IPv4 had to hide lots of devices behind one address (NAT). IPv6 has so many addresses that every device gets its own, so you use firewalls and privacy techniques instead of a shared door.

sections.title: IPv6 Protection Tools
sections.content:
IPv6 provides several key features that replace NAT's benefits. Privacy addresses (RFC 3041) generate temporary addresses that change over time, making it harder for outside parties to track a device across the Internet. The interface identifier part of the address randomizes, so a device using privacy addresses becomes difficult to correlate with earlier transactions.

Unique Local Addresses (ULAs) serve as private address space similar to RFC 1918 in IPv4. They are globally unique but not advertised on the public Internet, allowing networks to operate independently of their ISP and to be merged without address conflicts. ULAs use the FC00::/7 prefix.

DHCPv6 Prefix Delegation (DHCP-PD) allows ISPs to automatically assign address prefixes to customer routers, which then distribute them to local devices using stateless address autoconfiguration. This provides address management without translation.

Untraceable IPv6 addresses randomize subnet allocation so external observers cannot deduce network topology from addresses. By assigning addresses seemingly at random, the internal structure becomes invisible from outside.
sections.eli5: Privacy addresses are like wearing a different disguise each day. Unique Local Addresses are like having an internal postal code. Prefix delegation is like letting each household generate its own addresses. Untraceable addresses scramble the house layout so nobody can guess the map.

sections.title: Simple Security and Firewalls
sections.content:
IPv6 security does not depend on address translation. Instead, networks use stateful firewalls with reflexive access control, which allow outbound connections and return traffic but block unsolicited inbound connections. This provides the same practical protection that NAT's stateful filtering offers.

The size of IPv6 subnets (/64 subnets with 64 bits of address space for hosts) makes network scanning far more expensive than in IPv4. An attacker scanning an entire IPv6 /64 subnet would need to send about 5,000 years worth of packets at full-rate 40 Gbps. This makes topology probing and ping sweeps impractical.

IPv6 also makes IPsec more practical than with IPv4. NAT breaks IPsec in many scenarios, but in IPv6, end-to-end encryption and authentication can work without complications. Hosts can initiate connections from either direction, and transparent authentication is possible between any endpoints.

However, security is not automatic. A firewall must be configured correctly, and applications themselves must remain robust against attacks. NAT provides some indirect security benefit from obscurity, but this is not a substitute for proper security architecture.
sections.eli5: Instead of hiding behind NAT, you use a firewall that only lets messages in if you asked for them. IPv6 addresses are so big that trying every one to find targets would take thousands of years. Real encryption can work end-to-end without NAT breaking it.

sections.title: Practical Network Scenarios
sections.content:
Large enterprises can use IPv6 with ULAs for internal stability and global addresses for Internet access. Privacy addresses protect hosts from external tracking. When topology hiding is needed, they can use untraceable addresses assigned via a Home Agent (similar to Mobile IPv6), which appears from outside as if all hosts connect at the network edge.

Small networks and home users receive a prefix from their ISP via DHCP-PD, which allows every host to have a public address and full port access. If privacy is desired, hosts can enable privacy address generation. Unlike IPv4 homes that often share one address via NAPT, IPv6 homes can have a flat hierarchy where every device is independently reachable.

Single-user connections receive an entire /64 prefix, not a single address. This provides sufficient address space for privacy addresses and multiple interfaces if needed.

ISPs can provide IPv6 prefixes to customers without address translation, simplifying their infrastructure. They can filter traffic at the edge if policy requires it, but without the operational complexity of NAT.
sections.eli5: Big companies use private addresses inside and public ones outside. Homes get a whole block of addresses so every device has its own. Single users get enough addresses to change them whenever they want. ISPs don't need to translate anything.

sections.title: Remaining Work and Conclusions
sections.content:
This document identifies several gaps where additional standardization is helpful. The interaction between DHCP and Interior Gateway Protocols for address assignment needs better documentation. Dynamic pinhole management for firewalls requires further work. Privacy address use with topology masking needs best practices guidance. Site multihoming remains technically challenging even in IPv6, though architectural approaches are emerging.

Overall, IPv6 Local Network Protection demonstrates that the perceived security and management benefits of NAT can be achieved through explicit mechanisms without address translation. This preserves end-to-end transparency, allows applications to work properly, and gives administrators more explicit control over network behavior.
sections.eli5: Some details still need standards work, like firewall pinhole management. But the main point is proven: you can be safe and organized in IPv6 without hiding behind a shared front door.
